s11.quote: Princes of Thebes, two wayfarers as one,
s11.note: He greets Θήβης ἄνακτες (_Thebes anaktes_, "lords of Thebes", l. 988) in the plural: the elders and Creon together, where everyone else today has addressed Creon alone. The road he has walked is κοινὴν ὁδὸν (_koinen hodon_, "a shared road"). Keep the word _koinos_ in mind; in thirty lines he will say that error too is common to all men.

s11.quote: Having betwixt us eyes for one, we are here.
s11.note: The Greek uses the dual, ἐξ ἑνὸς βλέποντε (_ex henos bleponte_, "the pair of us seeing from one", l. 989), a grammatical form reserved for two things that make a pair. Sophocles used it in the prologue for the two sisters and the two brothers, and every one of those pairs has been broken. The blind man who sees truly is an old device, and Sophocles gave it to this same prophet again in the Oedipus. What matters here is that Teiresias knows he needs a guide and says so in his first sentence. Creon does not know it yet.

s11.quote: Why tidings, old Teiresias?
s11.note: 'Why' is a misprint for 'What'. The Greek asks what is νέον (_neon_, "new", l. 991), a word that in tragedy usually smells of trouble. Notice that the seer arrives unsummoned. In the Oedipus he has to be sent for twice; here he comes of his own accord, which tells you how bad the signs are.

s11.quote: And when thou hearest thou must heed the seer.
s11.note: "I will teach, and you obey": πιθοῦ (_pithou_, l. 992) is the imperative of the verb that means both "be persuaded" and "obey". Creon has spent the play demanding this of others and refusing it himself, most recently with Haemon in [[s7]]. Hold on to the word, because at l. 1099 he will finally say it back in the first person.

s11.quote: Thus far I ne’er have disobeyed thy rede.
s11.note: 'Rede' is counsel, but the Greek is more inward: he has never stood apart from the seer's φρενός (_phrenos_, "mind", l. 993). The line gives Creon a past in which he was a ruler who took advice, and it shows how far he has travelled since morning. It also sets a trap for him. If he has always followed this mind before, on what ground will he refuse it now?

s11.quote: So hast thou steered the ship of State aright.
s11.note: The ship of state was Creon's own figure in his inaugural speech in [[s3]], and "straight" was his favourite word there. Teiresias hands both back to him, but in the imperfect tense: ἐναυκλήρεις πόλιν (_enauklereis polin_, l. 994) is "you were captaining the city". Storr's perfect, 'hast steered', lets the good course run up to the present. The Greek leaves it in the past.

s11.quote: I know it, and I gladly own my debt.
s11.note: Literally, "I can testify from experience to benefits": ὀνήσιμα (_onesima_, "profitable things", l. 995). So Creon himself opens the scene's ledger of profit, and in an innocent sense: the seer's advice has paid. Within forty lines the same idea will come back as an accusation of bribery.

s11.quote: The razor edge of peril.
s11.note: The first word of the Greek line is the command φρόνει (_phronei_, "think", l. 996), the verb the whole play has been circling and will end on. Then ἐπὶ ξυροῦ τύχης (_epi xyrou tyches_), "on the razor of fortune", a Homeric phrase for the moment when things can still fall either way. That is the point of it. Teiresias is not announcing a doom; he is saying that Creon is balanced and can still step off on the right side.

s11.quote: Thy words inspire a dread presentiment.
s11.note: "I shudder at your mouth": φρίσσω (_phrisso_, l. 997) is the physical word, hair standing up. The man who has feared nothing all day is afraid before he has heard a single fact. I would mark this for later, when his collapse seems too quick. The fear is here from the start, and the bluster that follows is laid over it.

s11.quote: Sitting upon my throne of augury,
s11.note: The παλαιὸν θᾶκον ὀρνιθοσκόπον (_palaion thakon ornithoskopon_, "ancient bird-watching seat", l. 999) was a real place; Pausanias, centuries later, was still shown Teiresias' observatory at Thebes. He calls it a λιμήν (_limen_, "harbour") for every bird, a calm word chosen to be violated in the next line. Note the method of the speech: two separate techniques of divination, birds and then fire, are tried in turn and both fail.

s11.quote: A jargon strange of twitterings, hoots, and screams;
s11.note: Storr turns into an aviary what the Greek puts in two savage words. The birds scream in a frenzy, οἴστρῳ (_oistroi_, the gadfly's sting, l. 1002), and their cry is βεβαρβαρωμένῳ (_bebarbaromenoi_), "barbarized", turned into a foreign language. Bird-cry is the tongue a seer reads. He is saying that the language between gods and men has become gibberish.

s11.quote: So knew I that each bird at the other tare
s11.note: ἔγνων (_egnon_, "I knew", l. 1004): the blind man knows by ear what the sighted would have had to see. And what he hears is creatures of one kind tearing each other with their claws, which is the story of the two brothers played again in the air. In the entry song in [[s2]] Polyneices was the eagle screaming over Thebes; now the birds that fed on him have caught his war.

s11.quote: I straight essayed the sacrifice by fire
s11.note: The second test, made because he was afraid: δείσας (_deisas_, "in fear", l. 1005), where Storr has the milder 'Perturbed in soul'. ἐμπύρων (_empyron_) is the technical term for reading omens in the way an offering burns. A good prophet checks one method against another before he troubles a king.

s11.quote: On blazing altars, but the God of Fire
s11.note: Ἥφαιστος οὐκ ἔλαμπεν (_Hephaistos ouk elampen_, "Hephaestus did not shine", l. 1007). The altars are παμφλέκτοισιν (_pamphlektoisin_, "fully kindled"), so there is nothing wrong with the fire. It is the offering that will not take. The god's name stands for the flame, and the refusal is therefore a god's refusal.

s11.quote: And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze;
s11.note: Greek sacrifice was meant to send clean fat-smoke up to the gods; this one only weeps. The phrase is μυδῶσα κηκὶς (_mydosa kekis_, "a dank ooze", l. 1008), and the participle is the very word (_mydon_) the Guard used in [[s5]] for the rotting body of Polyneices. The altar is doing what the corpse is doing. Storr does not spare us and should not: the play insists that the offence is a bodily fact and no point of etiquette.

s11.quote: Melted and fell and left the thigh bones bare.
s11.note: In a proper sacrifice the thigh bones are wrapped in fat, καλυπτῆς (_kalyptes_, "covering", l. 1011), and burn inside it; that wrapped bundle is the gods' share. Here the covering slides off and the bones ἐξέκειντο (_exekeinto_), "lay exposed". It is the vocabulary of a body laid out, and the Chorus will use its cousin of Polyneices at l. 1101. The failed offering is a small model of the crime: something that ought to be covered lies bare.

s11.quote: Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read—
s11.note: ἐμάνθανον (_emanthanon_, "I was learning", l. 1012): the oldest and wisest man in Thebes learns from a child and is not ashamed to say so. Set that against Creon's sneer to Haemon in [[s7]], that men of his age are not to be schooled by a boy. The scene is built to show what Creon could not do.

s11.quote: As I guide others, so the boy guides me—
s11.note: ἡγεμών (_hegemon_, "leader, guide", l. 1014) is a word of command, and Teiresias gives it to the boy. Authority in his account is a chain in which everyone who leads is also led. Creon's account in [[s7]] had a single link: the man the city appoints must be obeyed in small things and great, just and unjust.

s11.quote: The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb.
s11.note: ἀσήμων ὀργίων (_asemon orgion_, "rites that give no sign", l. 1013). Nine lines earlier the whirr of wings was "not without meaning", οὐκ ἄσημος (_ouk asemos_, l. 1004); the birds meant something, and what they meant is that the rites now mean nothing. A tutor's question: has Teiresias received a message from the gods? Strictly, no. He has received the absence of one, and reasons from that.

s11.quote: O King, thy willful temper ails the State,
s11.note: The Greek is blunter and has no 'O King': "it is from your mind that the city is sick", νοσεῖ πόλις (_nosei polis_, l. 1015), with ἐκ φρενὸς (_ek phrenos_) naming the organ. The _phren_ that Creon said at l. 993 he had never departed from is now set against his own. Disease is the scene's master image from here on: Teiresias will tell Creon he is full of it at l. 1052, and the Chorus will sing of it in [[s12]].

s11.quote: By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows,
s11.note: Be exact about what is polluted. It is the βωμοὶ (_bomoi_, altars) and ἐσχάραι (_escharai_, hearths), and παντελεῖς (_panteleis_), all of them without exception (l. 1016). They are "full" of βορᾶς (_boras_, "carrion-meat", l. 1017), scraps of the dead man carried there by birds and dogs. Creon's edict promised exactly this feeding in [[s3]]; he did not think about where the animals would go afterwards. The pollution is public and material: the places where the city talks to its gods are fouled.

s11.quote: The flesh of Oedipus’ unburied son.
s11.note: Teiresias will not say 'traitor' and does not even use the name. The dead man is δυσμόρου (_dysmorou_, "ill-fated", l. 1018), "the fallen son of Oedipus"; 'unburied' is Storr's addition. To the prophet he is an unlucky member of an unlucky house, which is how Antigone saw him. Creon's political category has simply dropped out of the description.

s11.quote: Therefore no birds trill out a happy note,
s11.note: εὐσήμους (_eusemous_, "of good sign", l. 1021), the third _sema_ word in twenty lines. The traffic between Thebes and the gods is blocked in both directions: prayers and thigh-smoke do not go up (ll. 1019-20), and signs do not come down. The cause is stated physically. The birds have eaten the fat of a slain man's blood, so the instruments of prophecy are themselves contaminated.

s11.quote: O ponder this, my son. To err is common
s11.note: τέκνον, φρόνησον (_teknon, phroneson_, "child, think", l. 1023). The king is called child, and told for the second time to use his mind. Then the generous move: error is κοινόν (_koinon_, "common", l. 1024) to all, the same word as the shared road of his entrance. Teiresias is making it as easy as he can for Creon to back down without disgrace, and Haemon tried the same door in [[s7]].

s11.quote: The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise.
s11.note: Medical language again: the man who ἀκῆται (_aketai_, "heals", l. 1027) the harm and does not stay ἀκίνητος (_akinetos_, "immovable"). Such a man is no longer ἄβουλος (_aboulos_, "ill-counselled") or ἄνολβος (_anolbos_, "unblest"); Storr's 'wastrel' for the second is a strange choice, since the word concerns fortune and not thrift. This is the doctrine of the play in a sentence: the fault is ordinary, and what ruins a man is refusing the remedy while there is time.

s11.quote: No fool, the saw goes, like the obstinate fool.
s11.note: No proverb is announced in the Greek. The line is a verdict: αὐθαδία (_authadia_, "self-will", literally pleasing oneself, l. 1028) ὀφλισκάνει (_ophliskanei_), "is convicted of", stupidity, the stupidity being _skaiotes_, left-handed clumsiness. The verb is a law-court term for losing a case. The man who has acted as judge all day hears the language of sentence turned on himself.

s11.quote: Let death disarm thy vengeance. O forbear
s11.note: Storr dissolves the key word. The Greek says εἶκε τῷ θανόντι (_eike toi thanonti_, "yield to the dead man", l. 1029), and yielding is what Haemon begged for with his bending trees and slackened sail in [[s7]]. The same verb returns at l. 1096 when Creon breaks. Then κέντει (_kentei_, "stab, goad"): do not go on stabbing one who has perished.

s11.quote: By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well;
s11.note: ἐπικτανεῖν (_epiktanein_, "to kill over again", l. 1030), and he asks what ἀλκὴ (_alke_, "prowess") there is in it. This is the plainest objection to the edict, and it has taken until now for anyone to voice it: the man is already dead. The appeal is to Creon's soldierly pride, since _alke_ is a warrior's virtue and there is none in fighting a corpse.

s11.quote: Counsel’s most welcome if I promise gain.
s11.note: The last word of the speech is the fatal one: κέρδος (_kerdos_, "gain", l. 1032). Teiresias means it honestly, that it is pleasant to learn from a good adviser when the advice profits you. But _kerdos_ has been Creon's obsession since he accused the guards of taking bribes in [[s3]], and he hears only the sense he always hears. I think Sophocles makes the seer hand him the word so that we can watch what he does with it.

s11.quote: Like anchors at a target; yea, ye set
s11.note: 'Anchors' is a slip in this printing for 'archers': τοξόται σκοποῦ (_toxotai skopou_, "archers at a mark", l. 1033). Who are the 'all'? Antigone, Ismene, Haemon, the muttering city, and now the seer; in Creon's mind they have merged into one conspiracy. Teiresias takes up the image at the end of the scene and tells him that these arrows will not miss.

s11.quote: Your soothsayer on me. Peddlers are ye all
s11.note: Two commercial verbs carry the Greek: ἐξημπόλημαι κἀμπεφόρτισμαι (_exempolemai kampephortismai_, l. 1036), "I have been sold off and loaded as cargo", and by the whole tribe of seers. Creon has one theory of opposition and it is always the same: somebody has been paid. He applied it to the guards in [[s3]], and now applies it to the one man in Thebes whose record he has just vouched for.

s11.quote: Go to, and make your profit where ye will,
s11.note: The imperative is the verb of _kerdos_ itself (_kerdainete_, "make your gains"), followed by ἐμπολᾶτε (_empolate_, "trade away", l. 1037). Within six lines of the seer's honest use of the word, Creon has turned it into a sneer. Ask what the seer could possibly gain by Polyneices' burial. Creon never says, because the charge is a reflex and has no content.

s11.quote: Silver of Sardis change for gold of Ind;
s11.note: Not silver. The Greek is ἤλεκτρον (_elektron_, l. 1038), electrum, the pale natural alloy of gold and silver that came from the river at Sardis and made Lydia rich, paired with Indian χρυσόν (_chryson_, "gold", l. 1039). The geography belongs to Sophocles' own century more than to heroic Thebes. Creon reaches for the far ends of the world to say that no price would be enough, which shows how large the imagined bribe has grown.

s11.quote: Ye will not purchase this man’s burial,
s11.note: 'Purchase' is Storr keeping the trade metaphor going. The Greek is flat: "you shall not hide that man in a grave", τάφῳ (_taphoi_) and οὐχὶ κρύψετε (_ouchi krypsete_, l. 1039). Even now he will not name Polyneices; he is 'that one'. This is the edict's last restatement, and it is addressed to a prophet who has just told him the gods reject it.

s11.quote: Not though the winged ministers of Zeus
s11.note: The blasphemy. Storr's 'winged ministers' is polite; the Greek says the αἰετοὶ (_aietoi_, "eagles", l. 1040) of Zeus might snatch the body as βορὰν (_boran_, "carrion", the seer's word from l. 1017) and carry it ἐς Διὸς θρόνους (_es Dios thronous_, "to the thrones of Zeus", l. 1041). He has taken the report of fouled altars and raised it to the highest altar there is. Earlier he only slighted Zeus of the household when he condemned his niece; now he pictures rotting flesh on the god's seat and says he would not care.

s11.quote: Not e’en in awe of prodigy so dire
s11.note: Storr's 'prodigy' hides the word that matters: μίασμα (_miasma_, "pollution", l. 1042). Creon says he would not flinch from this as a pollution and so allow the burial. He names the thing precisely and refuses to fear it. Yet at the end of [[s7]] he was careful to leave food in Antigone's cave so that the city should escape exactly this stain. He believes in pollution when the belief costs him nothing.

s11.quote: No human soilure can assail the gods;
s11.note: 'Soilure' is defilement: θεοὺς μιαίνειν (_theous miainein_, "to pollute gods", l. 1044) is beyond human strength. The thought would be respectable in a philosopher, and it sounds like the enlightened talk of Sophocles' own day. But it answers something Teiresias never said. He did not claim the gods were stained. He said the altars were, and that the gods had stopped listening. Creon uses a sound piece of theology as permission to go on fouling their altars.

s11.quote: Of craft and cunning when it tries to gloss
s11.note: The clever who fall are πολλὰ δεινοὶ (_polla deinoi_, "formidable in many things", l. 1046), the adjective of the great ode in [[s4]], where man was the most _deinos_ of all creatures and his cleverness could carry him to ruin as easily as to greatness. Creon means the seer. The sentence describes Creon: a very able man about to take a shameful fall for speaking ugly things well.

s11.quote: Foul treachery with fair words for filthy gain.
s11.note: His speech ends where the seer's did, on τοῦ κέρδους χάριν (_tou kerdous charin_, "for the sake of gain", l. 1047). Two speeches, the same last word, opposite meanings: one man offers profit, the other can only hear corruption. Storr's 'filthy' is his own; the Greek puts the shame in the words spoken and leaves the gain bare.

s11.quote: Alas! doth any know and lay to heart—
s11.note: Teiresias begins a sentence and Creon cuts across it; the question is completed two lines later. Sophocles splits one thought over the line-for-line exchange so that we hear the interruption. The verb φράζεται (_phrazetai_, "considers", l. 1048a) asks whether anyone thinks things through, and the man opposite proves the answer by not letting him finish.

s11.quote: Is this the prelude to some hackneyed saw?
s11.note: πάγκοινον (_pankoinon_, "common to everyone", l. 1049): Creon sneers that a platitude is coming. He is right, and the platitude is true, and the play will end with the Chorus reciting it over him. The word is another _koinos_ compound, and it returns in the hymn of [[s12]] for the folds of Eleusis that receive all comers.

s11.quote: How far good counsel is the best of goods?
s11.note: εὐβουλία (_euboulia_, "good counsel", l. 1050) is ranked best of κτημάτων (_ktematon_, "possessions"). Since Creon will talk of nothing but property, the seer puts wisdom in the terms of property. The word comes back at l. 1098, when the Chorus tells Creon it is the one thing he now needs to get.

s11.quote: True, as unwisdom is the worst of ills.
s11.note: Creon caps the maxim correctly: μὴ φρονεῖν (_me phronein_, "not thinking straight", l. 1051) is the greatest harm. He can recite the moral of his own tragedy and has no idea it applies to him. The Chorus' closing lines in [[s13]] say exactly this, that good sense is the chief part of happiness.

s11.quote: Thou art infected with that ill thyself.
s11.note: νόσου πλήρης (_nosou pleres_, "full of that disease", l. 1052). The adjective is the one used of the altars at l. 1017, πλήρεις (_plereis_), full of carrion. The altars are full of the corpse and the king is full of the sickness; the two conditions are one, and the city's illness has been traced to a single patient.

s11.quote: I will not bandy insults with thee, seer.
s11.note: A flicker of the old respect. He still calls him 'the seer' and says he does not want to answer abuse with abuse. It lasts one line, and Teiresias will not let him keep the pose.

s11.quote: And yet thou say’st my prophesies are frauds.
s11.note: The seer points out that the insult has already been delivered: to say he prophesies ψευδῆ (_pseude_, "falsehoods", l. 1054) is the worst thing one can say of a prophet. The Chorus will answer this word directly at l. 1094, where they testify that he has never once spoken a falsehood to the city.

s11.quote: Prophets are all a money-getting tribe.
s11.note: φιλάργυρον γένος (_philargyron genos_, "a silver-loving breed", l. 1055). The Greek audience knew venal diviners, and the gibe had a real target in their world. It has none here, and Sophocles has taken care that we know it, since Creon admitted at l. 995 that this prophet's advice had always served him. Oedipus will make the same charge against the same man in the later play, and be just as wrong.

s11.quote: And kings are all a lucre-loving race.
s11.note: Teiresias returns the compound with interest: αἰσχροκέρδειαν (_aischrokerdeian_, "shameful gain", l. 1056), and he says it of τυράννων (_tyrannon_), which Storr softens to 'kings'. So _kerdos_ finally lands on Creon. What is his shameful profit, given that no money is involved? I take it to be winning: he would rather keep his victory over a dead man and a girl than keep the city clean.

s11.quote: Dost know at whom thou glancest, me thy lord?
s11.note: He pulls rank, as he did with Haemon and the Guard. The word is ταγοὺς (_tagous_, "commanders", l. 1057), a military title, in a lofty plural. When Creon runs out of argument he always reaches for the fact of his office.

s11.quote: Lord of the State and savior, thanks to me.
s11.note: ἐξ ἐμοῦ (_ex emou_, "through me", l. 1058) you hold this city, σώσας (_sosas_, "having saved it"). This is the debt acknowledged at l. 995, now called in. The play does not say what the earlier counsel was. Eurydice's dying reproach about Megareus in [[s13]] suggests it cost Creon a son, in which case the prophet who is about to take his second son once required his first.

s11.quote: Skilled prophet art thou, but to wrong inclined.
s11.note: A remarkable concession in mid-quarrel: σοφὸς σὺ μάντις (_sophos su mantis_, "you are a skilled seer", l. 1059). Creon never doubts the art, only the man's honesty. That is why he collapses so quickly once the prophecy is spoken. He has already granted that this prophet knows.

s11.quote: The mystery deep hidden in my breast.
s11.note: τἀκίνητα (_takineta_, "the things that should not be moved", l. 1060). At l. 1027 the seer warned against being ἀκίνητος (_akinetos_), immovable. Because Creon would not move, what ought to have stayed unmoved is now stirred up. Note what this implies about the first speech: Teiresias came with a diagnosis and a cure and was holding the worst in reserve.

s11.quote: Say on, but see it be not said for gain.
s11.note: κίνει (_kinei_, "move it, then", l. 1061): Creon orders the prophecy himself, with one more jab about κέρδεσιν (_kerdesin_, "profits"). Here is the question the scene leaves us with. Would the doom have been spoken, or even fixed, if he had yielded at l. 1032? The seer's talk of a cure implies it was still avoidable then. The prophecy that follows has no 'unless' in it.

s11.quote: Such thou, methinks, till now hast judged my words.
s11.note: Storr guesses at a difficult line. The Greek (l. 1062) is closer to "So indeed I think I shall speak, τὸ σὸν μέρος (_to son meros_), as far as you are concerned". That is, you say 'not for gain', and you are right: what I am about to tell you will bring no gain to you. It is a grim joke on Creon's word, and Storr's version misses it.

s11.quote: Be sure thou wilt not traffic on my wits.
s11.note: "Know that you will not trade in τὴν ἐμὴν φρένα (_ten emen phrena_, "my mind")" (l. 1063). His last word before the prophecy is the commercial metaphor again, and its object is the very _phren_ the seer diagnosed at l. 1015 as the source of the city's sickness. He is defending the diseased organ as though it were his treasure.

s11.quote: Know then for sure, the coursers of the sun
s11.note: κάτισθι (_katisthi_, "know it well", l. 1064) throws back Creon's "be sure" from the line before; the seer answers a command to know with a stronger one. The Greek has no horses, only τρόχους ἁμιλλητῆρας ἡλίου (_trochous hamilleteras heliou_, "the racing wheels of the sun"). Not many circuits, he says. In the event the sun does not complete one.

s11.quote: Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins
s11.note: σπλάγχνων (_splanchnon_, l. 1066) is "inward parts, guts", and Storr's 'loins' makes it decorous. These are also the parts a sacrificer handles and a seer inspects. After a speech about an offering the gods would not accept, Creon is told that one will be taken from his own body. The Greek adds "one"; as [[s13]] will show, the count is low.

s11.quote: In quittance of thy murder, life for life;
s11.note: The terms of the prophecy, and Storr blurs them. The Greek is νέκυν νεκρῶν ἀμοιβὸν (_nekyn nekron amoibon_, "a corpse in exchange for corpses", l. 1067), with ἀντιδοὺς (_antidous_, "paying over in return"). There is no 'murder' in the line and no 'life'. One dead body is owed for dead bodies in the plural, which counts the living Antigone as already a corpse. And the idiom is that of payment. Creon wanted to talk about buying and selling, and this is the bill.

s11.quote: For that thou hast entombed a living soul,
s11.note: ψυχήν (_psychen_, "a life", l. 1069) has been lodged in a tomb ἀτίμως (_atimos_, "without honour"). The verb κατῴκισας (_katoikisas_) is the one used for settling people in a new home, as a founder settles colonists. Creon has made a household in a grave, and the phrase picks up Antigone's own bitter address to her tomb as a bridal chamber and dwelling in [[s9]].

s11.quote: And sent below a denizen of earth,
s11.note: The indictment in five words: τῶν ἄνω βαλὼν κάτω (_ton ano balon kato_, "having thrown below one of those above", l. 1068). A 'denizen of earth' is someone who belongs up here among the living. The sentence then balances it with its mirror: he keeps up here one who belongs below. Notice that Antigone comes first. The seer's first speech was all about the corpse; the charge of burying the living is new, and it stands at the head of the sentence.

s11.quote: A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered.
s11.note: Three negatives in a row: ἄμοιρον, ἀκτέριστον, ἀνόσιον (_amoiron, akteriston, anosion_, l. 1071). Storr keeps the hammering and changes the sense. The words are "without his portion", "without funeral rites", "unhallowed"; there is no washing or weeping in them, and 'unwept' is borrowed from Antigone's own triplets earlier in the play. The first is the important one. The dead man has been denied his share, and the gods below theirs, since the line says he belongs to them.

s11.quote: Herein thou hast no part, nor e’en the gods
s11.note: An argument about jurisdiction. In the dead neither Creon nor the gods above have any share, μέτεστιν (_metestin_, l. 1072); the upper gods βιάζονται (_biazontai_, "are being forced", l. 1073) by him. That is an astonishing thing to say: Creon is doing violence to the Olympians by leaving on their ground what is not theirs. This is why I resist the tidy scheme, usually credited to Hegel, of two equal rights colliding. The prophet does not weigh state against family. He says a boundary in the order of things has been crossed, twice.

s11.quote: For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell
s11.note: The Ἐρινύες (_Erinyes_, l. 1075) are named, of Hades and of the gods together, so both worlds send them; Storr's 'Hell' brings in a Christian place the Greek does not know. They are ὑστεροφθόροι (_hysterophthoroi_, "destroying late", l. 1074) and they λοχῶσιν (_lochosin_, "lie in ambush"). The Chorus sang of a Fury in the mind in [[s6]] as the thing that ruins this family. Now Furies wait for Creon, who is of the family only by marriage and thought himself outside its curse.

s11.quote: What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too.
s11.note: Literally, he is to be caught "in these same" κακοῖς (_kakois_, "evils", l. 1076). Storr's 'these' wavers between the victims and the gods. I read it as exact retribution in kind. He put the living among the dead, and he will end as what the Messenger in [[s13]] calls a breathing corpse; he kept the dead from their own, and he will stand holding his own dead.

s11.quote: And now, consider whether bought by gold
s11.note: κατηργυρωμένος (_katergyromenos_, "silvered over", l. 1077), plated with silver like a cheap object made to look precious. It is the seer's last reply to the charge of bribery, and it is contemptuous. He does not argue the point. He says: wait a little, and judge by what you hear in your house.

s11.quote: Of men and women through thy desolate halls;
s11.note: ἀνδρῶν γυναικῶν (_andron gynaikon_, "of men, of women", l. 1079), set side by side without a conjunction, and their κωκύματα (_kokymata_, "shrieks of mourning"). Creon has built his position on the difference between these two words: no woman shall rule him, better to fall to a man. The prophecy levels them in one sound. The cry is the kind Antigone raised over her brother's body in [[s5]], and it will come from his own doors. 'Desolate' is Storr's; the Greek says only "your house".

s11.quote: And all thy neighbor States are leagues to avenge
s11.note: 'Leagues' is a slip for 'leagued'. The cities are stirred up ἐχθραὶ (_echthrai_, "in enmity", l. 1080): Creon's whole policy rested on sorting friend from enemy, and it has made him enemies abroad. These four lines widen the crime to all the Argive dead left on the field, the story Euripides tells in his Suppliants. They sit oddly in a play that has spoken of one corpse only, and some editors have suspected them. If they stand, they show the edict as policy, applied to a whole army.

s11.quote: I’ the maw of wolf or hound, or winged bird
s11.note: The verb Storr passes over is the bitter one: the dogs καθήγνισαν (_kathegnisan_, "consecrated", l. 1081) the torn remains. It is the proper word for performing funeral rites. The only burial these men received was in the bellies of animals, and Teiresias says so in the vocabulary of the ritual they were refused.

s11.quote: That flying homewards taints their city’s air.
s11.note: The bird carries an unholy ὀσμὴν (_osmen_, "smell", l. 1083) to a city that is ἑστιοῦχον (_hestiouchon_, "possessing the hearth"). So what happened to the altars and hearths of Thebes at l. 1016 is happening in every city that lost men here. Pollution in this play does not stay where it is put. It travels on wings, and the image of the gorged bird ties the end of the prophecy back to the birds that opened the first speech.

s11.quote: These are the shafts, that like a bowman I
s11.note: τοξότης (_toxotes_, "archer", l. 1084) answers Creon's complaint at l. 1033 that everyone shoots at him: very well, here are τοξεύματα (_toxeumata_, "arrows"), and sure ones. Notice that he admits to anger, θυμῷ (_thymoi_, l. 1085), and says "for you hurt me". A prophet who is stung and strikes back is an uncomfortable figure. I think Sophocles wants us uneasy about how much of the doom was drawn out by the quarrel.

s11.quote: On younger men, and learn to curb his tongue
s11.note: Let him vent his temper on νεωτέρους (_neoterous_, "younger men", l. 1088). The audience has just watched him do it to Haemon. The closing line (l. 1090) asks for a better νοῦν (_noun_, "mind") than the φρενῶν (_phrenon_, "wits") he now carries, so the seer's exit, like his entrance and his diagnosis, is about Creon's thinking. He leaves as he came, led by the boy, and Creon has said nothing.

s11.quote: My liege, that man hath gone, foretelling woe.
s11.note: δεινὰ θεσπίσας (_deina thespisas_, "having prophesied terrible things", l. 1091). The word _deinos_, which the ode in [[s4]] made so double-edged, has only its dark side left by this point in the play. There is a silence to imagine before this line: Creon alone with the elders, and they are the ones who speak first.

s11.quote: The prophet’s warning to the State to fail.
s11.note: Never has he uttered a ψεῦδος (_pseudos_, "falsehood", l. 1094) to the city, which is a direct reply to Creon's charge at l. 1054. This is the moment the Chorus finally commits itself. They have hinted, hedged, and deferred all day; they once wondered aloud whether the burial was the gods' work and were silenced. Now they speak as the collective memory of Thebes, grey-haired men who have watched this prophet for a lifetime.

s11.quote: I know it too, and it perplexes me.
s11.note: The turn, eleven lines after the seer's exit: ἔγνωκα (_egnoka_, "I have recognised it", l. 1095) and ταράσσομαι φρένας (_tarassomai phrenas_, "I am shaken in my mind"). Ask what did it. Not argument: Haemon gave him better arguments and he threatened to kill the girl in front of him. What moves him is fear, and the authority of a prophet whose skill he conceded at l. 1059. I think the speed is the point. A will this rigid breaks all at once.

s11.quote: To yield is grievous, but the obstinate soul
s11.note: εἰκαθεῖν (_eikathein_, "to yield", l. 1096), the verb of Haemon's trees and the seer's "yield to the dead", is at last in Creon's mouth, and he calls it δεινόν (_deinon_, "terrible"). He uses the same adjective for the alternative in the next line. That is his predicament exactly: two terrible things, and he has only now noticed the second.

s11.quote: That fights with Fate, is smitten grievously.
s11.note: There is no 'Fate' in the Greek. What he fears is to resist and strike his spirit against ἄτῃ (_atei_, l. 1097), _ate_, the ruinous delusion the Chorus sang of in [[s6]] as the thing a god sends on the man he means to destroy. Creon has heard that ode's lesson and names his danger correctly. He names it too late, which is how _ate_ works.

s11.quote: Son of Menoeceus, list to good advice.
s11.note: εὐβουλίας (_euboulias_, l. 1098), the 'best of possessions' from l. 1050, and the Chorus says he must "get hold of" it, as of something he does not have. They address him by his father's name and as παῖ, 'child'. For the third time in the scene the king is spoken to as a son who needs teaching.

s11.quote: What should I do. Advise me. I will heed.
s11.note: The speaker label in this printing says CHORUS, but the line is Creon's. Its last word is πείσομαι (_peisomai_, "I will obey", l. 1099), the answer, a hundred lines late, to the seer's opening πιθοῦ at l. 992. It is the first time all day that he has asked anyone what to do. The man who told his son that the ruler must be obeyed in everything now takes orders from the elders he summoned to be an audience.

s11.quote: Go, free the maiden from her rocky cell;
s11.note: The order is fixed by the grammar: κόρην (_koren_, "the girl", l. 1100) with the particle that means 'first', the tomb with the one that means 'and then'. The living first, then the dead; it is the obvious order, since a corpse can wait and a girl in a cave cannot. It is also the order of the seer's indictment at l. 1068. Watch what Creon does when he reaches the plain.

s11.quote: And for the unburied outlaw build a tomb.
s11.note: 'Outlaw' is Storr's. The Chorus says only τῷ προκειμένῳ (_toi prokeimenoi_, "for him who lies exposed", l. 1101), the ordinary word for a body laid out before burial. No traitor, no enemy, no name. The political description of Polyneices, which the elders accepted in [[s3]], has gone from their speech as it went from the seer's.

s11.quote: Is that your counsel? You would have me yield?
s11.note: παρεικαθεῖν (_pareikathein_, "to give way", l. 1102). He promised one line ago to obey, and his first response to the advice is to query it. I hear disbelief more than resistance: he cannot quite credit that these deferential old men are telling him to surrender. Each such line costs time, and time is now the only thing that matters.

s11.quote: Is swift to overtake the impenitent.
s11.note: Storr's 'impenitent' is Christian colouring. The Greek is κακόφρονας (_kakophronas_, "the wrong-thinking", l. 1104), another _phronein_ compound: the gods' harms, βλάβαι (_blabai_), are ποδώκεις (_podokeis_, "swift-footed") and cut off those who think badly. The warning about speed is right and already out of date. Antigone has been in the cave since before the last ode.

s11.quote: My heart’s resolve; but Fate is ill to fight.
s11.note: He stands out of his own heart, ἐξίσταμαι (_existamai_, l. 1105), and the reason he gives is ἀνάγκῃ (_anankei_, "necessity", l. 1106), against which one must not fight. Storr again writes 'Fate'. Mark what the yielding is and is not. He does not say he was wrong, or that Antigone was right, or that the dead have claims. He says he is compelled. Recognition of the fault comes only in [[s13]], over the bodies.

s11.quote: Go, trust not others. Do it quick thyself.
s11.note: The elders have noticed how Creon rules: through guards, through proclamations, through other men's hands. Everything he has ordered today was carried out by someone else. Now he must go in person, and the Messenger's report will show him on his knees at the mouth of the cave.

s11.quote: My henchmen! Get ye axes! Speed away
s11.note: He shouts for servants "present and absent", which is the speech of a man who has lost his composure. Why ἀξίνας (_axinas_, "axes", l. 1109)? The cave was sealed with stones, and an axe is no tool for that. They are presumably for cutting wood, and the Messenger will speak of fresh-cut boughs on Polyneices' pyre. So even as he gives the order, his mind is on the burial.

s11.quote: To yonder eminence! I too will go,
s11.note: ἐπόψιον τόπον (_epopsion topon_, "the place in full view", l. 1110) is the high ground where the body lies; the Guard's men sat on the hilltops there in [[s5]]. He sends his men to the corpse. The destination he names first is the second item in the Chorus' instructions.

s11.quote: ’Twas I that bound, I too will set her free.
s11.note: ἔδησα (_edesa_, "I bound") and ἐκλύσομαι (_eklysomai_, "I will release"), with παρὼν (_paron_, "being there in person", l. 1112). This is what he says he will do, and it matches the Chorus' order. What he does, as [[s13]] reports, is go first to Polyneices, wash and burn and bury him with full rites, and only then turn to the cave, where he is minutes too late. Whether the reversal kills her is a real question. I think it is in character: he sees to the city's pollution and the gods' claim before the person. And he has always supposed that what he tied he could untie.

s11.quote: Almost I am persuaded it is best
s11.note: Storr softens the verb. Creon says δέδοικα (_dedoika_, "I am afraid", l. 1113) that it may be best. Fear governs the sentence; he has not been persuaded of anything. That is the measure of his change at this point, and it is why the scene leaves me uneasy. He has given up his position, but nothing suggests he has understood why it was wrong.

s11.quote: To keep through life the law ordained of old.
s11.note: τοὺς καθεστῶτας νόμους (_tous kathestotas nomous_, "the established laws", l. 1113). His first speech in [[s3]] made _nomos_ mean his own proclamation; Antigone answered in [[s5]] with the unwritten ordinances that no one can date. He now concedes her ground in her vocabulary, without naming her. The Greek says to keep them until one's life ends, and his exit line therefore finishes on the word for ending a life.

s12.quote: Thou by many names adored,
s12.note: πολυώνυμε (_polyonyme_, "you of many names", l. 1115) is the proper opening of a Greek prayer: name the god fully, list his haunts, then ask him to come. The ode keeps to that form, two stanzas of places and then the request. Why do the elders sing hope here? Because from where they stand the problem is solved. The king has yielded, the prophet's cure is being applied, and all that is left is to ask the city's own god to finish the cleansing. The audience can count the minutes Creon has lost and knows better.

s12.quote: Child of Zeus the God of thunder,
s12.note: Zeus is βαρυβρεμέτα (_barybremeta_, "deep-thundering", l. 1116), and the epithet is chosen with care, since it was that thunder which killed the god's mother. Storr has reversed the Greek order, where the mortal bride comes first and Zeus second. The elders begin from the Theban side of the god's parentage because their claim on him runs through it.

s12.quote: Of a Theban bride the wonder,
s12.note: Καδμείας νύμφας ἄγαλμα (_Kadmeias nymphas agalma_, "glory of the Cadmean bride", l. 1115). An _agalma_ is a thing one delights in and also a precious object offered to a god. The bride is Semele, daughter of Cadmus. Three women in this play are brides in a bad sense: Semele consumed by her bridegroom, Antigone married to her tomb, and Eurydice, who is about to come out of the palace doors.

s12.quote: Fair Italia’s guardian lord;
s12.note: Ἰταλίαν (_Italian_, l. 1118) is the Greek south of Italy, vine country, where Athens was helping to found the colony of Thurii at about the time this play is usually dated. Some editors have wanted to read an Attic place-name here, on the ground that Italy is a long way to go in a Theban hymn. I would keep it. The catalogue is meant to sweep from the far west home to Thebes.

s12.quote: Of the Eleusinian Queen
s12.note: Δῃοῦς (_Deious_, "of Deo", l. 1120) is Demeter, and her κόλποις (_kolpois_, "folds, bosom") are the sheltered plain of Eleusis, which Storr makes into glades. They are παγκοίνοις (_pankoinois_, "common to all", l. 1119) because the Mysteries took anyone who came. It is the word Creon used at l. 1049 to sneer at a commonplace. Eleusis matters for another reason: its rites concerned what happens to the dead. The god invoked to heal Thebes has one foot in the world below, where the offence was committed.

s12.quote: Where the Dragon’s teeth were sown,
s12.note: The σπορᾷ (_sporai_, "sowing", l. 1125) of the savage δράκοντος (_drakontos_, "serpent"): Cadmus sowed the teeth and armed men grew, who at once killed one another. Thebes begins in kin-slaughter, and the play began the morning after two brothers repeated it. In [[s2]] the dragon stood for the city that beat off the Argive eagle. Here it is simply part of the address, the ground the god is asked to walk on.

s12.quote: Thebes, O Bacchus, is thine own.
s12.note: He is Βακχεῦ Βακχᾶν (_Baccheu Bacchan_, "Bacchus of the Bacchants", l. 1120) and dwells in Thebes their ματρόπολιν (_matropolin_, "mother-city", l. 1121). Dionysus was born of a Theban princess, which makes him family, and the elders are calling in a relative. It is the second time they have done so. The entry song in [[s2]] ended with Bacchus invited to lead the victory dances through the night, and that night has not yet come.

s12.quote: Thee on the two-crested rock
s12.note: The διλόφου πέτρας (_dilophou petras_, "twin-peaked rock", l. 1126) is Parnassus above Delphi, which Dionysus was held to occupy in the winter months when Apollo was away. What sees him there is λιγνύς (_lignys_, l. 1127), the smoky flare of torches. Flame and smoke going up from a mountain to a god: after the seer's account of altars that would not burn, the picture is of a sacrifice that works.

s12.quote: Where Corisian maidens flock,
s12.note: Storr's 'Corisian' should be Corycian: Κωρύκιαι (_Korykiai_, l. 1127), the nymphs of the great cave high on Parnassus, here called Bacchic. A cave full of dancing girls who honour a god is an uncomfortable thing to sing while a girl hangs in another cave not far from the city. I doubt the elders hear it. I am sure Sophocles did.

s12.quote: By Nysa’s bastion ivy-clad,
s12.note: Νυσαίων ὀρέων (_Nysaion oreon_, "the Nysaean hills", l. 1131). Nysa was the mountain where the infant god was nursed, and every region that grew vines claimed one; the strait mentioned later suggests the Euboean Nysa is meant, just across the water from Boeotia. Ivy and grape-clusters are his plants. The slopes "send" him, so the god is pictured already on his way.

s12.quote: And through our streets we Thebans shout,
s12.note: Storr gives the shouting to the Thebans. In the Greek the cries are "immortal" and the god is the one acting: he is watching over the ἀγυιάς (_agyias_, "streets", l. 1135) of Thebes, the verb being the one from which we get 'overseer'. He is addressed by the same title at l. 1147. The elders want inspection, a god who walks the streets and sees what is wrong in them.

s12.quote: Oh, as thou lov’st this city best of all,
s12.note: ὑπερτάταν πόλεων (_hypertatan poleon_, "highest of cities", l. 1137) in his honour. The great ode in [[s4]] said the man who keeps the laws of the land and the justice of the gods stands high in his city, and the reckless man has none. The Chorus still thinks of Thebes as the city that stands high. Their ground for asking is the god's partiality, which is how Greek prayer works: you have favoured us before, do so now.

s12.quote: To thee, and to thy Mother levin-stricken,
s12.note: 'Levin' is an old word for lightning: ματρὶ σὺν κεραυνίᾳ (_matri syn kerauniai_, "with your thunder-struck mother", l. 1138). Semele asked to see Zeus as he is and was burned up by the sight. Even the city's patron comes out of a story about a mortal woman destroyed by contact with the divine. The elders mean it as an honour. In this play, on this day, it reads as a warning about what divine attention costs.

s12.quote: Thou see’st with what a plague our townsfolk sicken.
s12.note: No epidemic has been mentioned anywhere. The νόσου (_nosou_, "disease", l. 1141) is the seer's word from l. 1015 and l. 1052, and the Chorus has taken over his diagnosis entire: the πάνδαμος πόλις (_pandamos polis_, "the city with all its people") is gripped by it. They call it βιαίας (_biaias_, "violent", l. 1140), which recalls the seer's charge that the gods themselves were being forced. One man's order has made everyone unclean. What they do not say is whose mind the sickness came from.

s12.quote: Thy ready help we crave,
s12.note: The Greek is much more precise than Storr's general plea. He is asked to come καθαρσίῳ ποδὶ (_katharsioi podi_, "with cleansing foot", l. 1142), which is to say dancing, and to purify. This is the irony of the whole ode. A healing is prayed for and the next person through the entrance is the Messenger. The cleansing does come, and it takes the form of three deaths and a king emptied out. The play does not tell us whether to call that the god's answer or his silence.

s12.quote: Or o’er the roaring straits thy swift was wending,
s12.note: The printing is garbled; read 'thy swift way wending'. The strait is στονόεντα πορθμόν (_stonoenta porthmon_, l. 1145), and the adjective means "groaning, full of moans" more than 'roaring'. It is the Euripus between Euboea and the mainland. In a hymn of joy the god's road home is given the epithet of lamentation, a few lines before the house fills with the wailing Teiresias foretold.

s12.quote: Save us, O save!
s12.note: Storr's cry is not in the Greek, which asks only that the god μολεῖν (_molein_, "come", l. 1142). Sophocles does this more than once: he places a song of excited hope directly before the catastrophe, in the Ajax, the Oedipus and the Women of Trachis as well as here. It is a deliberate use of the Chorus' limited view. They are decent, pious, and one step behind events, and their joy raises the height from which the next scene falls.

s12.quote: Brightest of all the orbs that breathe forth light,
s12.note: Storr makes the god a star. The Greek makes him the chorus-leader of the stars, those ἄστρων (_astron_, l. 1146) that are πῦρ πνειόντων (_pyr pneionton_, "breathing fire"). The whole night sky is imagined as a dancing chorus with Dionysus at its head. A chorus of old men in the god's own theatre is asking the leader of a greater chorus to come and take over the dance.

s12.quote: Authentic son of Zeus, immortal king,
s12.note: After the titles comes the one verb the hymn has been working towards: _prophanethi_, "appear", show yourself. Greek hymns often end by asking for an epiphany, and tragedies sometimes grant one, with a god on the roof in the last scene. This play does not. No god appears in Antigone at any point, and everything divine is reported, inferred, or read from signs.

s12.quote: Leader of all the voices of the night,
s12.note: νυχίων (_nychion_, "of the night", l. 1146) and φθεγμάτων ἐπίσκοπε (_phthegmaton episkope_, "overseer of voices", l. 1147). It is a strange and lovely title, and a reminder of how long this one day has run since two sisters met before sunrise. The night voices the elders mean are the cries of the god's worshippers. The voices this night will actually hold are the ones the seer promised at l. 1079, men and women wailing in Creon's house.

s12.quote: Come, and thy train of Thyiads with thee bring,
s12.note: The Θυίαισιν (_Thyiaisin_, l. 1151) are the women who ran on Parnassus for Dionysus, and they are called his περιπόλοις (_peripolois_, "attendants", l. 1150). Storr's later 'Thy handmaids we' is his own; the elders do not claim to be the god's women. Still, it is notable that a play so anxious about women out of doors and out of control ends its last ode by asking for a troop of them.

s12.quote: Thy maddened rout
s12.note: μαινόμεναι (_mainomenai_, "raving", l. 1151). Madness has been a term of abuse all day, thrown at Antigone by Creon and at Creon by nearly everyone. In [[s2]] the attacker who came against Thebes with fire was described as raging like a bacchant. Here the same frenzy is holy and wished for. The ode does not reconcile the two, and I do not think it can. Dionysus is the god in whom destruction and blessing have one face.

s12.quote: Who dance before thee all night long, and shout,
s12.note: πάννυχοι χορεύουσι (_pannychoi choreuousin_, "they dance all night", l. 1151) repeats the all-night dances the elders proposed at dawn in [[s2]]; the play's two great hymns to Bacchus frame the day. The last words are τὸν ταμίαν Ἴακχον (_ton tamian Iakchon_, l. 1152). Iacchus is his Eleusinian name, the cry of the initiates' procession, and _tamias_ is a steward, one who gives out portions. The dance never happens. The name is still in the air when a man walks on and begins to speak of a fortune overturned.
